title: Get, Give, and Encourage Guidance
hook: Who loses the chance to improve when a kind silence keeps the hard fact back?
counterintuition: The gentle delay can be the cruel move. When you hide useful truth to keep the hour smooth, the person who needed it pays later.
tryThisNow: Ask one person within 5 minutes, "What is one thing I do that makes your job harder?" Then write the answer in one sentence.
keyTakeaway: Begin by asking for criticism, give specific praise and correction while it can still change the result, and help peers speak directly before comfort turns missing truth into lost time.

breakdown.fastRead:
What would Kim Scott lose if Sheryl Sandberg kept the hard observation to herself? The public account places their management relationship in a Google-era workplace, with 2017 as the anchor. The beat is small and costly: one person can spend an awkward minute, or the other person can miss the truth that would help.

Ruinous Empathy is care without direct challenge. In plain words, it is kindness that protects comfort and hides needed information. Guidance culture means praise and criticism moving toward the boss, from the boss, and among peers. Start by asking for criticism before giving it. Then give specific praise and correction. Then help peers speak to each other. Direct guidance is not a harsher mood. It is useful truth while change is still possible.
breakdown.deepRead:
The hard fact lands as help only when the receiver can see care. That is why the order starts with asking, not telling. Before you correct another person, ask what you are missing. You pay first. A repeated question lowers the price of speaking up because the answer no longer has to break the social rules on its own.

Sandberg and Scott show why the hard line is not a script. Sheryl Sandberg and Kim Scott are the real people in the Google-era direct-feedback case; the public account anchors it in 2017. The important part is not a famous senior leader's style. The important part is that trust already exists, so a hard observation can arrive as help rather than humiliation.

The failure case is Bob. Juice Software is the early-company setting in Radical Candor where delayed criticism leads toward firing. The first loss is information. Bob cannot fix what he has not been told in plain terms. The second loss is time. Each soft pass lets the problem get larger. The third loss is fairness: when the final talk comes, it carries truth that should have been spread over earlier moments.

Who paid for the quiet? Bob did, and so did the people around the problem. Ruinous Empathy is care without direct challenge. It feels kind at the instant of delay. It is not kind if the person loses a chance to improve.

The order is simple but not easy: solicit feedback, give feedback to individuals, then encourage feedback between peers. Praise counts too. Specific praise tells someone what to repeat; vague approval only tells them you are pleased. The lesson is a working note on delayed criticism. Every unspoken fact has a bill, and the bill often lands on the person you meant to spare.
breakdown.fullRead:
Bob's failure starts before firing is on the table. It starts at the first soft pass. The person with the hard fact chooses comfort, so Bob keeps moving without the plain signal that something has to change.

Step one is hidden data. A vague hint makes Bob guess. If he guesses wrong, the miss looks stubborn instead of uninformed. Step two is lost time. The same issue returns, and the later talk has to carry more weight than it should. Step three is a thinner sense of fairness. By the time firing is near, the useful truth sounds like a verdict.

That is the cruel twist. The kind-looking move can shift pain from you to the person who needed the fact. Short comfort becomes long cost.

Juice Software gives the failure a name and a place without turning it into company folklore. Bob is the cautionary case for delayed criticism leading toward firing. This lesson does not ask you to enjoy bluntness. It asks you to stop treating delay as protection.

The Sandberg thread shows the narrow cure. Sheryl Sandberg and Kim Scott provide a real Google-era relationship for direct guidance; trust is already part of the scene. That matters because the same hard observation can land in two ways. With care, it can help. Without care, it can feel like a public loss of face even when the content is true.

Do not overcorrect into Obnoxious Aggression. That label means direct challenge without care: the fact may be right, but the person has little reason to believe you are helping. Do not duck into Manipulative Insincerity either. That is neither care nor direct challenge; the person protects image or advantage, so truth moves through side channels. Silence is not neutral there.

Guidance culture means praise and criticism moving up, down, and sideways. The official order is solicit feedback, give feedback to individuals, then encourage feedback between team members. Ask first. Use one question often enough that people can prepare a real answer. Give feedback to one person with a fact they can act on. Then encourage peers to speak directly, because they often see the task before the boss does.

Specific praise belongs in the same system. If you only say that something was good, the person gets warmth but not guidance. If you name the behavior that worked, the person knows what to repeat. Praise without a clear referent can hide needed information too.

The limit is carried by the failed versions. If you have not shown that you can receive criticism, a call for peer candor can sound like you are exporting discomfort. If your hard line has no care signal, accuracy can still damage trust. If you hold back because you want to be liked, the silence may turn political. The move is not "be more honest." It is ask first, speak with care, and give the fact early enough to use.

You can do it without a title. Ask for one critique of your part. When you praise, tie it to a behavior. When you correct, say the fact before the window closes. When two people route the same issue through you, ask what one fact they should carry to each other.

The Bob lesson is not that firing is always wrong or that comfort is always suspect. The lesson is stricter: late truth can turn a fixable gap into a final talk. A kind delay is still a delay. The person you meant to spare may be the one who pays.

examples.title: Before the Result

planSpec.stakes: a useful fact could arrive as help or humiliation
planSpec.requiredBeat: state the standard before anyone knows the result

examples.scenario: What would you ask before copying Sandberg's directness? Ask whether the relation can carry the hard observation. In the real Google-era case, Sheryl Sandberg states a demanding point to Kim Scott inside a trusted management relationship. The outcome is not claimed here. The proof is earlier: directness is not free-standing.
examples.whatToDo: Can the other person read your line as help? If trust is thin, ask for criticism of yourself before you raise the standard.
examples.whyItMatters: What gets protected when you wait for trust? The person's ability to use the fact without feeling reduced by it.

examples.title: The Spent Minute

planSpec.stakes: the correction works only if the awkward cost is paid
planSpec.requiredBeat: show the move working after the demand has already landed

examples.scenario: Kim Scott is already taking in Sheryl Sandberg's hard observation inside the Google-era relationship; the standard has been set. A brief silence does the expensive work. The move works because the relation can bear the hard point, and because Sandberg does not trade the useful fact for a smoother minute. The cost is immediate discomfort. The gain is usable guidance.
examples.whatToDo: Which cost is yours? Spend the awkward minute while the fact is still useful. Do not move the price to the other person by waiting.
examples.whyItMatters: What changes after the minute is spent? The hard observation stays tied to help, and comfort no longer hides information.

examples.title: Ask Before Correcting

planSpec.stakes: credibility is lost if criticism flows only downward
planSpec.requiredBeat: answer the earlier commitment to solicit feedback

examples.scenario: At the promised follow-up, the earlier commitment comes due: solicit feedback before giving it. The answer is thin, and the would-be critic nearly treats that as permission to start correcting others. The sequence pulls the miss back just in time. Ask again, get one usable criticism, then give feedback to individuals.
examples.whatToDo: Which question proves you can receive truth? Ask it again before you correct anyone else, and wait for one usable answer.
examples.whyItMatters: What proof does criticism need? Show humility first; otherwise your candor push begins as a one-way demand.

examples.title: Bob's Late Price

planSpec.stakes: late truth turns a fixable gap into a firing path
planSpec.requiredBeat: trace the late outcome back to unclear feedback

examples.scenario: After the damage is visible, Bob's Juice Software story runs backward. The path toward firing did not begin with the final talk; it began with delayed criticism that kept the real issue blurred. Each soft pass made the later conversation carry more weight. The account stops before it asks you to judge the ending. It asks you to price the delay.
examples.whatToDo: What does skipping cost first? It costs the person useful time. Say the behavior that must change before the talk narrows to a final choice.
examples.whyItMatters: Who carries the late bill? Bob does, because unclear feedback postponed the real conversation and made the problem harder for everyone.

examples.title: Past the Bottleneck

planSpec.audience: people who see the issue first
planSpec.stakes: routing every hard truth through one boss slows learning
planSpec.requiredBeat: show the effect first outside the boss path

examples.scenario: The Order of Operations feedback sequence first shows its effect away from the boss path. Before solicit feedback and give feedback to individuals, every concern waits for one clearinghouse; after encourage feedback between team members, peers who see the task first carry the fact to each other. The cost is loss of control for the boss.
examples.whatToDo: Why does the peer step work? Peers often see the task first; encourage them to speak with the fact instead of routing every issue upward.
examples.whyItMatters: What price does the boss pay? Less control. The payoff is faster learning and fewer hidden queues for hard truth.

examples.title: Praise With a Signal

planSpec.stakes: vague approval hides what should be repeated
planSpec.requiredBeat: show vague praise headed for a miss, then pull it back

examples.scenario: What is quietly failing if praise in the Sheryl Sandberg and Kim Scott Google-era thread stays warm but vague? The recipient hears approval, yet loses the repeatable fact. On page 33, Radical Candor names the danger of comfort without direct challenge. The miss is pulled back when praise names the behavior to repeat before the moment fades.
examples.whatToDo: Which praise lets the person repeat the move? Name the observed behavior, not your warm feeling about the result.
examples.whyItMatters: What miss does this prevent? Vague approval protects ease but hides the signal that would improve a later pass.

questions.prompt: A clinic lead keeps a weak habit comfortable until the aide loses a key shift. Which earlier move would have changed the result?
choices: Ask the senior clinician to deliver the message later, so the truth has rank behind it when the loss is official.
Keep the aide calm until the schedule resets, then explain the pattern once the pressure is lower.
Name the missed behavior while the aide can still use it, with enough care that the line lands as help.
questions.explanation: The harm is useful truth arriving too late. The senior-clinician choice borrows rank after the loss, while the right move gives the aide timely information with care.

questions.prompt: When a volunteer coordinator hears only polite approval, which first step best lowers the cost of upward criticism?
choices: Wait for a helper to volunteer a concern, then treat that first brave answer as proof the door is open.
Ask only after a visible mistake, so the request feels tied to a concrete reason instead of rank.
Use the same plain question on a steady rhythm, so helpers can prepare an honest answer before they are put on the spot.
questions.explanation: A repeated question makes criticism easier to prepare. Asking only after a mistake fires the right move too late and turns candor into an event response.

questions.prompt: If a principal admires Sandberg's directness and wants to copy the blunt style with a new aide, what maps from the case?
choices: Use a sharper line first, then let the aide learn that high standards are how trust gets built.
Build enough trust that a hard observation can register as help, not as a public put-down, before the line arrives.
Borrow a respected educator's wording, so the aide hears the correction as proven practice rather than personal opinion.
questions.explanation: The relationship is part of the mechanism. Borrowed wording sounds safer, but it treats the case as style rather than a trusted relation carrying hard truth.

questions.prompt: After a library project stalls, every concern waits for the branch supervisor even when clerks saw the snag first. What was missed?
choices: Collect the concerns privately, then decide which clerk deserves the clearest correction from the supervisor.
Have the clerks address the fact with each other, because peers often see the task first.
Wait for the supervisor to model a perfect sentence, then have the clerks repeat that wording.
questions.explanation: The missed step is peer feedback. Private collection keeps the supervisor as clearinghouse, which is the bottleneck this move removes.

questions.prompt: A studio founder lets a weak pattern slide because the designer seems fragile. Why is that default costly?
choices: Unclear feedback postpones the real conversation, so the pattern grows harder for the designer and the studio.
A warmer praise line has not been found yet, so the designer lacks confidence before hearing the concern.
The founder should send the issue through a peer first, since direct criticism from the founder is the main risk.
questions.explanation: The Bob case teaches the cost of delay: unclear feedback lets the problem grow. Warmer praise may help some moments, but it cannot replace the missing correction.

questions.prompt: Before a department head starts asking everyone to be more candid, which action earns the first credibility?
choices: Give each staff member one crisp correction, so the campaign begins with a shared standard that everyone can see.
Ask staff to correct one another first, so the head can watch whether honesty travels sideways.
Solicit criticism of the head's own behavior, so later correction does not look like a one-way demand.
questions.explanation: Get before give proves receptiveness. Starting with downward correction may be clear, but it skips the humility that makes later criticism more credible.

questions.prompt: A committee member sees a serious flaw, says nothing in the session, then warns allies afterward. What caused the trust damage?
choices: The member challenged too directly before showing care, so the accurate point sounded harsher than needed in front of everyone at the table.
The member protected image or advantage, so feedback became political instead of useful while the flaw stayed hidden from the full group.
The member gave specific praise in the session, so the later flaw seemed smaller than it was to the people who needed warning.
questions.explanation: The damage comes from evasion and side-channel warning. The harshness answer would fit Obnoxious Aggression, but here the person avoided direct challenge.

questions.prompt: During a lab handoff, a true criticism leaves the assistant shut down rather than clearer. What best explains the miss?
choices: The lead challenged without a care signal, so accuracy damaged trust instead of helping the assistant use the point.
The assistant needed the repeated upward-feedback question before hearing any specific praise or correction.
The lead should have routed the criticism through a peer, because the main problem was who delivered it rather than whether it carried care.
questions.explanation: A true point can still fail when care is absent. The peer-routing option aims at the wrong target; the problem shown is delivery without a care signal.

questions.prompt: Your writing partner improves one paragraph, and you want the move repeated later. Which response fits the lesson?
choices: Praise the exact behavior that worked, so your partner knows what to repeat.
Save detail for the later critique, so the praise stays easy to hear and does not turn into correction.
Ask a senior writer to approve the praise, so the standard feels less personal and more established.
questions.explanation: Specific praise is guidance because it marks repeatable behavior. Saving detail for critique makes praise warm but vague, which is the error this card avoids.

reviewCards.front: What comes before you give hard criticism?
reviewCards.back: Ask for criticism of yourself. Getting before giving proves that truth can travel upward, not only toward the person with less power.
Care becomes unfair when it hides needed information. The person feels spared in the moment but loses time to improve.

reviewCards.front: What does Bob's Juice Software case warn you about?
reviewCards.back: Delayed criticism can move a fixable problem toward firing. The cost is not just discomfort later; it is lost useful information earlier.

reviewCards.front: Why is specific praise part of guidance?
reviewCards.back: Specific praise tells someone what to repeat. Vague approval may feel good, but it does not mark the behavior that made the result better.

reviewCards.front: What makes the Sheryl Sandberg and Kim Scott case unsafe to copy as mere style?
reviewCards.back: The trusted Google-era relationship is part of the mechanism. Copying bluntness without that base can turn a useful hard observation into humiliation.

reviewCards.front: When should truth stop routing through the boss?
reviewCards.back: When peers see the task first, they should often carry the fact to each other. Routing every issue upward slows learning and creates dependence.

implementationPlan.title: Ask the Useful Question
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Ask the Useful Question. Use one repeated question to invite criticism before you give any. Then write the behavior you will praise or correct while the other person can still use it. The skill is not sharper speech; it is timely information with care.

ifThenPlans.context: You are tempted to delay criticism to keep the hour smooth.
ifThenPlans.plan: If I want to delay criticism, then I will ask, "What fact would help them change while it still matters?"

ifThenPlans.context: Someone gives only polite approval when you ask for input.
ifThenPlans.plan: If I hear only polite approval, then I will ask, "What is one thing I do that makes your job harder?"

ifThenPlans.context: A peer issue keeps coming through you.
ifThenPlans.plan: If two peers keep routing the same issue through me, then I will ask, "What fact should you take to each other?"

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before tomorrow ends, draft 1 exact ask you will use before a hard line: "What am I missing that would help you do better?"
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each Friday for 15 minutes, observe where comfort delayed a fact, then note the first question you will ask before the following week.

memorableLines.text: Direct guidance is not a harsher mood.
memorableLines.why: It redefines guidance away from tone and toward useful truth.

memorableLines.text: Every unspoken fact has a bill, and the bill often lands on the person you meant to spare.
memorableLines.why: It names the concrete price of delayed criticism.
It asks the sharp question behind short-term comfort.
